articles.title: US struck 60 targets as 40 vessels, 18mn barrels of oil crossed Hormuz in record day: Report
articles.summary: Middle East News: The US military escorted 40 commercial vessels carrying around 18 million barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, marking a wartime hi.
articles.body: The US military escorted 40 commercial vessels carrying around 18 million barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, marking a wartime high as Washington and Tehran exchanged a fresh round of strikes, according to two US officials familiar with the operation who spoke to CNN.The high-risk operation came as US forces simultaneously struck nearly 60 Iranian military targets around the strategic waterway, while defending the escorted vessels against waves of drone attacks and neutralising anti-ship cruise missiles.Before the war began just over six months ago, around 20 million barrels of oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz each day. But since the conflict began, shipping through the key waterway has slowed to a trickle, disrupting global energy markets and pushing up prices.The US operation involved a range of air, sea and space assets and was part of a broader strategy focused on controlling the strait, protecting commercial shipping and increasing economic pressure on Iran.The targets hit on Tuesday included air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites, the officials told CNN. US forces also continued a naval blockade of Iranian ports, with Central Command directed to focus its efforts on the strait and preventing oil exports from leaving or entering Iranian ports.The operation comes amid growing risks for commercial shipping. On Monday, a Saudi Arabia-flagged crude oil tanker came under attack and caught fire as it was preparing to cross the strait, killing two Filipino crew members. Fourteen other Filipino crew members survived.Iran has also stepped up attacks on US allies in the Gulf. Bahrain said its air defence systems intercepted several Iranian air attacks early Wednesday, while Iranian state media reported drone attacks on US bases in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.The escalation followed US strikes on Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. Washington said Iran was preparing to use the launchers to fire mines into the waterway. Iran retaliated by launching missiles at American bases in Jordan, which were intercepted.The US military’s latest operation, however, has not eased concerns among energy companies about sending ships through the strait, even under military escort. Energy prices remain elevated, adding to turbulence in global markets.At the same time, the administration’s other priorities have taken a back seat. According to one US official, operations aimed at eliminating elements of Iran’s nuclear programme have effectively been “backburnered”, as the focus shifts towards securing the waterway and restricting Iranian oil flows.Iranian media meanwhile reported that a US strike hit a home hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, killing four people and wounding at least 68. The US military said it was aware of the report but that it “never targets civilians.”With the conflict intensifying, diplomatic efforts are continuing. Egypt and Qatar have called for Washington and Tehran to return to negotiations, while Pakistan said it remains engaged in mediation efforts. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said Washington was pressuring countries still doing business with Iran, saying, “My message to everyone is stay away.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Minneapolis shooting kills two, wounds three police officers
articles.summary: Police say suspected gunman is also dead and that several people, including three officers, were wounded.
articles.body:
At least two people have been killed and several more wounded, including three police officers, after a gunman opened fire in the United States city of Minneapolis.

Garret Parten, a spokesman for the police, told reporters on Wednesday that the suspect has also died.

He said police responded to a call about a shooting at a downtown Minneapolis apartment building just after 4:30pm local time (22:30 GMT). Officers found the victims minutes after entering the high-rise.

One person died at the scene, Parten said. Four people were taken to hospital, where one later died.

Also taken to hospital were three police officers, including two who were shot. All three are in stable condition, according to Hennepin County Medical Center.

Parten said it was not immediately clear how the shooter died.

The police have no further details on the motive behind the shooting or the condition of those injured.

Video posted to social media showed police aiming weapons at an apartment building near the Minneapolis Convention Center.

In a series of posts on X, Minnesota Governor Tim Walz thanked emergency services and said state officials are on the ground helping local law enforcement respond to the shooting.

“Grateful to law enforcement actively working to ensure the safety of our neighbors in Downtown Minneapolis this afternoon,” Walz said.

“Minnesota is praying for our first responders.”

Minnesota House of Representatives Speaker Lisa Demuth said she is praying for the victims of “this heinous crime”.

The shooting in Minneapolis came on the same day that a shooting was reported at Westwood Hills Elementary School in the city of Waynesboro in the state of Virginia.

Authorities said a 19-year-old gunman forced his way into the elementary school on Wednesday morning and shot and wounded a staff member before killing himself.

The incidents follow mass shootings in the cities of Chicago, Illinois, and Trenton, New Jersey, on Sunday that left at least three people dead and 18 wounded, according to authorities.

articles.title: Virginia couple arrested after 5-year-old nonverbal daughter is found dead in South Carolina waters
articles.summary: John Herb Hayes III, 70, and Geordyn Nichole Hayes, 31, were charged with unlawfully placing a child at risk or willfully abandoning a child.
articles.body: A Virginia couple have been arrested after their 5-year-old daughter, described as autistic and nonverbal, was found dead in South Carolina waters this week. John Herb Hayes III, 70, and Geordyn Nichole Hayes, 31, of Bristol, were arrested Monday evening in Carter County, Tennessee, and charged with unlawfully placing a child at risk or willfully abandoning a child, the Georgetown County Sheriff’s Office announced. Their daughter, Saylor Hayes, was reported missing Sunday afternoon. Her body was found Monday morning in the waters near Hagley Landing, a boat ramp leading to the Waccamaw River in the small town of Pawleys Island, South Carolina, following an extensive search involving hundreds of people and multiple agencies. The arrest warrant affidavits for the parents say that on Sunday, they placed Saylor at risk of harm by “failing to provide supervision and safeguards appropriate for a severely nonverbal, autistic five-year-old child with known affinity to water and history of elopement.” The parents were being held at the Carter County Detention Center in Tennessee without bond pending an extradition hearing. It was not immediately clear Wednesday night whether they have attorneys. Authorities initially said Saylor’s mother reported that her child had wandered off from a rental home in Hagley Estates in Pawleys Island and was last seen wearing her swimsuit. Deputies said they were trying to track her with a Project Lifesaver transmitter, a wearable device that emits a frequency that law enforcement can track if the wearer goes missing. Saylor had been wearing a Project Lifesaver monitoring device since 2024, but it had been removed before the family left Virginia, the affidavits said. Then, once she was in South Carolina, Saylor was left unsupervised within 15 meters of a body of water, the filing said. After she disappeared, the parents encouraged search efforts to be directed toward using the tracker even though they knew Saylor was not wearing the device, and they also directed search efforts away from the nearby body of water, the affidavits said. Georgetown County Sheriff Carter Weaver called Saylor’s death “a heartbreaking tragedy” that has “deeply affected our community.” “Saylor was a vulnerable five-year-old child who depended upon the adults responsible for her care and protection,” he said in a statement. “She deserved to be safe. She deserved to be protected.” The Washington County Sheriff’s Office in Virginia said in a statement that it was the agency hosting the Project Lifesaver program that Saylor enrolled in back in June 2024. It said the program helps law enforcement find people at risk of wandering because of cognitive conditions or special needs. After Saylor disappeared Sunday, it said, the Georgetown County Sheriff’s Office reached out to request information about her Project Lifesaver transmitter. When searchers in South Carolina were unable to detect her frequency, the Washington County Sheriff’s Office was asked to check her home. When officers responded to the Hayes residence, they detected the frequency assigned to Saylor’s transmitter, which was inside a vehicle on the property, the sheriff’s office said. “The transmitter was not with Saylor when she went missing in South Carolina,” the agency added. The sheriff’s office noted that the transmitter is attached using a specialized band for continuous wear — “it cannot simply be unclasped or removed by the client; the band must be physically cut in order to remove the transmitter.” “Nothing we do can bring Saylor back,” said Weaver, the Georgetown County sheriff. “What we can do is pursue the truth, seek accountability through our justice system, and continue doing everything within our authority to protect the most vulnerable members of our community.”

articles.title: US military boards, searches and sinks vessel allegedly supporting Los Choneros narco-terrorists
articles.summary: Video captures USS San Antonio Marines boarding and sinking a Los Choneros narco-terrorist floating refueling station in the Eastern Pacific.
articles.body: The U.S. military on Wednesday intercepted and sank a vessel in the Eastern Pacific that it said was supporting a "narco-terrorist" organization, according to U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM). SOUTHCOM said the operation targeted a vessel tied to Los Choneros, which it described as a violent narco-terrorist organization. "On Sept. 2, at the direction of #SOUTHCOM Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan, and in coordination and collaboration with the Government of Ecuador, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere (JTF-WHEM) successfully interdicted a vessel operating as a floating refueling station in support of illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations in international waters of the Eastern Pacific," SOUTHCOM said in a statement. "Intelligence confirmed the vessel was operating in support of the Los Choneros violent narco-terrorist organization," the military added. WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES SOUTHCOM said U.S. Marines and sailors from the USS San Antonio "interdicted, boarded, searched, and cleared the vessel without incident." The military said multiple individuals were removed from the vessel and transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. Once the individuals were safely removed, U.S. forces sank the vessel, SOUTHCOM said. In its statement, SOUTHCOM said the operation "cuts off a critical node" in the alleged drug traffickers' illicit activities. It did not disclose the specific location of the operation. The action was taken in support of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (A3C) and JTF-WHEM's mission to dismantle narco-terrorist networks in the region, according to SOUTHCOM. US MILITARY LAUNCHES FIRST AUTONOMOUS WARFARE COMMAND TO DEPLOY UNMANNED SYSTEMS ACROSS LATIN AMERICA "We are taking decisive action to dismantle and destroy sophisticated logistics networks used by narco-terrorists to traffic drugs and spread violence throughout the Western Hemisphere," Donovan said. "This operation demonstrated the elite capabilities and precision of Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere, which is on watch in the region to apply total systemic friction on these networks," he added. Video of the operation released by SOUTHCOM shows military personnel intercepting the vessel before boarding it and ultimately sinking the craft. SOUTHCOM also responded after Ecuador's Ministry of National Defense shared footage of the operation on social media. DEM SENATOR ACCUSES PENTAGON OF MURDER WITH BOAT STRIKES TARGETING DRUG TRAFFICKERS "The message is clear: the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition will continue to apply total systemic friction on narco-terrorists," SOUTHCOM wrote. Wednesday's interdiction comes amid a monthslong campaign launched by the Trump administration aimed at dismantling cartel-linked trafficking networks. SOUTHCOM has conducted dozens of strikes in the Eastern Pacific and Caribbean targeting vessels it says are connected to "narco-terrorists." Last week, the military said it carried out a strike in the Caribbean that killed four alleged "narco-terrorists." Following that strike, the Trump administration's campaign targeting suspected cartel vessels has resulted in at least 227 deaths across 68 reported strikes over roughly one year. articles.title: Social media is Lindsay Clancy wild card that could tilt potential retrial to the defense, retired judge says
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's deadlocked jury received a Tuey-Rodriguez charge as a retired judge warns social media could give her defense an edge in a retrial.
articles.body: If Lindsay Clancy's murder trial ends in a mistrial, her defense could hold an unusual advantage in a retrial, a retired Massachusetts Superior Court judge says, as jurors reported for a second time Wednesday that they remain deadlocked. Clancy, 36, faces three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her children — Cora, Dawson and Callan, all under age 6 — who were found strangled at the family's home in January 2023. Judge William Sullivan gave jurors a Tuey-Rodriguez charge Wednesday afternoon after they reported for a second time that they were deadlocked, having first signaled they were stuck earlier in the week. The charge is given to a deadlocked jury to encourage they continue deliberations, but also to remind them to listen to one another without sacrificing their honestly held opinions. WHAT IS A TUEY-RODRIGUEZ CHARGE? JUDGE GIVES INSTRUCTION TO DEADLOCKED LINDSAY CLANCY JURY Sullivan declined to give the instruction earlier in the week when jurors first reported difficulty agreeing, opting instead to simply send them back. The jurors deliberating in Clancy's murder trial are discussing several options, which include first-degree murder, second-degree murder, voluntary or involuntary manslaughter, not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility (insanity) or not guilty. LINDSAY CLANCY VERDICT: RETIRED JUDGE EXPLAINS WHAT HAPPENS IF INSANITY DEFENSE PREVAILS Retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Jack Lu told Fox News Digital that a retrial after a mistrial has traditionally favored the prosecution, but that social media has upended that conventional wisdom. "In the past, the conventional wisdom was that the prosecution is more likely to win on a retrial after a hung jury. Now it's different... The new conventional wisdom is question mark because of social media infected trials," Lu said. LINDSAY CLANCY MURDER TRIAL BECOMES SOCIAL MEDIA OBSESSION AS TIKTOKERS, SLEUTHS DEBATE CONTROVERSIAL CASE Lu pointed to Karen Read's case, the Massachusetts woman who was tried twice in the death of her Boston police officer boyfriend. Her case drew a massive amount of social media interest, which he said had a major impact on her trials. In 2024, jurors deadlocked in Read's trial, and she was acquitted at her retrial in 2025. "In the Karen Read case, the social media abuse was at a slow boil in the first trial. At the second trial, it just all erupted," Lu said. LINDSAY CLANCY JURORS VISIT CRIME SCENE IN KAREN READ-STYLE MOVE TO TEST TIMELINE: RETIRED JUDGE Lu himself said he's no longer on social media because "it's too abusive an environment." articles.title: Xi visits Egypt as China seeks deeper influence across the Mideast
articles.summary: Chinese leader Xi Jinping aims to present China as a stabilizer in the region and contrast it with the regional military entanglements of the U.S., including the war with Iran.
articles.body: CAIRO — On the surface, Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt this week is a run-of-the-mill opportunity for two countries to strengthen economic and diplomatic ties. But there is deep subtext to the meeting between Xi and President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi: China, the United States’ top global rival, is cultivating an extensive relationship with one of America’s key allies in the Middle East as it moves to expand its influence in the rapidly changing region. Xi aims to present China as a stabilizer in the region and contrast it with the United States, which for decades has been militarily entangled there — its six-month war with Iran being just the latest example. “China continues to build up its soft power reserves while the United States self-sabotages its own stock,” Amr Hamzawy, director of the Washington-based Carnegie Middle East Program, wrote in a paper earlier this year along with Kathryn Selfe, a former fellow at the program. Xi arrived Tuesday evening at Cairo airport, which was adorned with Chinese and Egyptian flags. El-Sissi and military guards greeted him on the tarmac with a red-carpet ceremony. In wide-ranging talks Wednesday, Xi said Cairo and Beijing should jointly oppose what he called “unilateralism and acts of bullying,” according to Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency. The Chinese leader also called for the two countries to “work together for a more just and equitable global governance system,” Xinhua reported. Xi, who visited the Grand Egyptian Museum near the pyramids of Giza, is on his first trip to Egypt in a decade, the first time he has been in the region since visiting Saudi Arabia in 2022. El-Sissi has visited China multiple times in recent years. The leaders marked 70 years of diplomatic ties by publishing friendly opinion pieces on Tuesday in Egypt’s state-run newspapers. Xi wrote that Beijing and Cairo should “expand the scope of pragmatic collaboration” through development. El-Sissi lauded China’s investments in Egypt and reiterated Cairo’s support of China’s claim that Taiwan is part of its territory. Egypt views its growing relationship with China as a way to diversify its strategic partnerships. In 2023, Egypt was invited to join the BRICS bloc of nations, a grouping of major emerging economies that includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa and is seen as a counterbalance to Western-led institutions such as the G7. A year later, Egypt signed agreements with China to collaborate on its Belt and Road Initiative, a signature policy of Xi’s that seeks to build power and transportation infrastructure around the world. China has invested more than $10 billion in Egypt, building a business hub east of the capital, Cairo, and an electric rail line for industry in the Nile Delta. Annual trade between the two countries is estimated at $20 billion, according to government figures. Trade between the U.S. and Egypt was $15.7 billion in 2025. Egypt is a crucial partner in U.S. national security priorities in the region, and the countries’ leaders enjoy close ties. In 2023, Beijing brokered a deal to re-establish diplomatic ties between Iran — its most important regional ally and oil supplier — and Saudi Arabia, a longtime U.S. ally. The agreement showcased China’s aspirations to compete with the United States for influence in the Mideast. Since then, ties between Riyadh and Tehran have frayed. Iran attacked Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries as part of its retaliation against the U.S. and Israel, which launched the war on Feb. 28. China has cast itself as a regional mediator in other ways. It has long advocated a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which is seen by the Arab world as a linchpin to regional stability. Shortly before Hamas militants attacked Israel in 2023 and launched the war in Gaza, Xi had hosted Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and announced a “strategic partnership” with the Palestinian Authority. With oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz heavily disrupted by the Iran war, the Suez Canal — which is controlled by Egypt — has become an important alternative path for getting energy supplies out of the region. “China has good reason to strengthen ties with the country that controls the route still open,” said Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat, a Middle East expert with Jakarta’s Center of Economic and Law Studies. Xi views Egypt “as a base to reach the wider Arab and African world, at a time when the U.S. has less attention to spare there,” Rakhmat said. In August, China and Egypt held a multiday air exercise at several bases across Egypt — the first-ever combat exercise for China’s J-16 fighter jets and Egypt’s French-made Rafale fighters. Xi is visiting Cairo after attending a two-day conference of the 10-nation Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a political and security group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence. The leaders of Russia, India, Pakistan and Iran attended the conference in Kyrgyzstan’s capital, Bishkek.

articles.title: US’s Chevron, Italy’s Eni to expand oil projects in Venezuela
articles.summary: Energy firms sign deals in Caracas, days after Venezuela agreed to grant the US control of a fifth of its oil reserves.
articles.body:
Chevron and several other global energy companies have signed multibillion-dollar deals to boost Venezuela’s oil output at a ceremony in Caracas, overseen by interim President Delcy Rodriguez and United States Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

The deals on Wednesday are separate from a recently unveiled Caracas-Washington agreement that gives the US access to 17 Venezuelan oilfields, representing about a fifth of the country’s total reserves.

Most of the new contracts relate to project expansions that have been under negotiation with Venezuela’s Oil Ministry and ⁠state oil company PDVSA since a sweeping oil reform approved in January following the US’s abduction of former President Nicolas Maduro.

Wright, who had travelled to Caracas to oversee the signing ceremony, said the deals signed by Venezuela with the US’s Chevron and GE Vernova, as well as Italy’s Eni, were “critical in starting this ball rolling of peace, opportunity, and prosperity” in the country.

“We are trying to work at what I call Trump-speed. [US] President [Donald] Trump didn’t want a nudge or a slow drift in a positive direction,” Wright said. “He wanted to see as fast as possible transformation in Venezuela.”

The new contracts will see Chevron and Eni ramp up their operations in Venezuela while gaining greater stakes in the oil fields.

Chevron, the US’s second-largest oil company and the top private oil producer in Venezuela, has valued its deal to develop two additional oil fields in the Orinoco Belt at $7bn, and the project’s output will more than double in five years.

Eni said it had gained exclusive rights to explore the giant Junin 5 oilfield.

US energy company GE Vernova, an offshoot of General Electric, meanwhile, will help repair Venezuela’s battered electricity grid.

The ceremony took place amid growing questions about Venezuela’s sovereignty following the larger Caracas-Washington deal, which grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over the 17 oil fields in the country.

Critics in both the US and Venezuela accuse Trump of holding the country for ransom after abducting Maduro in a raid and warning that Rodriguez could face a similar fate if she does not fall into line with Washington’s demands.

But Wright insisted that the US was not “stealing Venezuelan oil”.

“All we’re doing is taking an idle, underground asset that isn’t doing anything for Venezuelan people, and bringing the money, the technology to develop it,” he told reporters on Wednesday.

Wright added that the total oil output in Venezuela, which holds the world’s largest proven oil reserves, will reach 2 million barrels per day (bpd) by the end of the decade, up from 1.25 million bpd today.

That would still be far off Venezuela’s peak of more than 3 million bpd in the late 1990s.

Rodriguez, meanwhile, denied she was surrendering her country’s riches, saying that cutting the US in on Venezuela’s oil wealth is necessary to secure investment in the oil sector.

More oil “translates into more jobs, higher wages, better public services, hospitals, schools and food”, she said.

Rodriguez has estimated that Venezuela will make $209bn in profit from the deals over 25 years.

The pivotal role in the deal, played by fraud-accused Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, has come under scrutiny. He was not seen at Wednesday’s ceremony.

Betancourt has been linked to a corruption scandal at state oil company PDVSA and runs North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), Venezuela’s second-largest private oil company, in which the US government is taking a 35 percent stake under the deal.

Wright on Wednesday defended NABEP’s “highly successful track record of producing large volumes of oil in Venezuela”, adding: “That’s a business partner you can believe in.”

The agreement is a major about-face for the “Chavismo” movement of late socialist firebrand Hugo Chavez, Maduro’s mentor, who nationalised Venezuela’s oil fields two decades ago on an anti-imperialist platform.

It has amplified fears that the Trump administration is entrenching former Maduro loyalists, like Rodriguez, who have shown no readiness to hold democratic elections eight months after Maduro’s overthrow.

Trump on Wednesday rebuffed calls from several Republican lawmakers for quick polls in Venezuela.

“I just don’t think they’re ready yet. You know, it’s very new. We took them out of a dictatorship, and we’re getting along great with the government,” he said.

Rodriguez took a similar line, saying there would be “an electoral process” when “Venezuela is ready”.

articles.title: Powerful storm hits Canada’s Toronto, cutting power to tens of thousands
articles.summary: Thunderstorm also causes severe flooding and forces flight cancellations at Pearson airport.
articles.body:
A powerful thunderstorm has hit Canada’s largest city, Toronto, damaging buildings, closing roads and cutting power to tens of thousands of residents.

The storm on Wednesday brought torrential rain, strong winds, and large hail, prompting tornado watches and warnings in some areas.

At least 45,000 customers were without electricity as of 8pm on Wednesday (00:00 GMT on Thursday), according to electricity provider Toronto Hydro.

The storm brought down trees and caused flooding, prompting road closures in the city, including on the Don Valley Parkway, the CBC reported.

The Michael Garron Hospital, located in Toronto’s East York community, said its emergency department has been affected by flooding.

Images published by the CBC showed cars nearly submerged in the city of Vaughan, north of Toronto.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said in a post on X that the city’s emergency operations centre has been activated since Wednesday morning.

“City crews are already out responding to downed power wires, fallen trees, flooding and more,” she said. The Toronto Transit Commission, which operates subways and buses, “is working to restore service where it has been affected by flooding and debris spread by high winds”, she added.

Dozens of flights set to depart Toronto Pearson International airport on Wednesday evening were either delayed or cancelled .

Canada’s weather agency, Environment and Climate Change Canada, lifted an orange warning for severe thunderstorms in the Greater Toronto Area.

But a yellow alert warning of heat and severe thunderstorms remained in place over parts of the southwestern Ontario province.

Actress Mia McKenna-Bruce is to be awarded an honorary doctorate by Canterbury Christ Church University for helping to "elevate Kent onto the national stage".

McKenna-Bruce, a former student at Maidstone Grammar School for Girls, will receive her award for services to acting, after beginning her career as a child when she featured in the CBBC series Tracy Beaker Returns and its spin-off The Dumping Ground.

The award will be given to her at a ceremony at the university later in September.

She has also starred in Agatha Christie's Seven Dials on Netflix as Lady Eileen "Bundle" Brent.

Also receiving an award from the university is Judith Armitt DL, who previously served as chief executive of Medway Council and Thames Gateway.

The university said that she helped it to work with the Universities of Kent and Greenwich to deliver the Universities at Medway.

She will get her honorary doctorate in recognition of her services to regional and public service, and outstanding contributions to the university.

Canterbury Christ Church University's vice-chancellor and principal, Prof Claire Ozanne, said: "We are delighted to award Judith and Mia honorary doctorates from Canterbury Christ Church University.

"Our graduation ceremonies give us a wonderful opportunity to celebrate these remarkable achievements, as well as those of our students and welcome them to our alumni community."

articles.title: Glasgow City Council at 'critical' point over £110m budget gap
articles.summary: The Accounts Commission warns "robust oversight" is needed to tackle a £110m budget gap spanning the next two financial years.
articles.body:
Glasgow City Council is facing a "critical" point in a bid to turn around its finances, Scotland's public spending watchdog has warned.

The Accounts Commission said "robust oversight" was needed to tackle a £110m budget gap spanning the next two financial years.

Its report found that other potential costs, over an ongoing equal pay dispute and the rising of cost of homelessness, could add to the budget pressures.

The commission said that decisions over the next few months would have a "significant bearing" on the council's future financial sustainability.

What impact do refugees have on housing in Glasgow?

The 2026 Best Value report found that the council had a £45.7m overspend from the 2024-25 financial year.

It said there were no "established longer term financial planning arrangements" and the city faced a combined £109.7m budget gap for 2026-27 and 2027-28.

The Accounts Commission highlighted that alongside high levels of poverty and deprivation, two key issues placed additional pressure on Glasgow's finances.

The first was the long-running issue of equal pay, which the commission said must be addressed quickly to avoid further significant financial impact.

Glasgow City Council previously paid out about £770m after it emerged female workers in roles such as catering or cleaning had for years been receiving up to £3 an hour less than those in male-dominated areas such as refuse collection.

It has committed to implement a new pay and grading structure from April 2027.

The Accounts Commission said meeting this deadline was "critical" in order to avoid further equal pay liabilities and a "financial and operational impact on the council".

The spending watchdog also said homelessness costs were adding "significant additional pressure", which is expected to cost the council £56m this year.

The growth in homeless applications has been linked to the asylum backlog .

After being granted leave to remain, asylum seekers are classed as refugees and must leave UK Home Office accommodation - at this point they can turn to local councils for assistance.

Last year, Glasgow City Council leader Susan Aitken said the city had "run out" of temporary accommodation for people declaring themselves homeless.

"We're having to put them up in hotels, and that's very, very expensive," she said.

The Accounts Commission also said Glasgow City Council must outline necessary choices to enable it to "live within its means".

It said cash reserves "continue to decline" and were below the council's own targets.

It advised the local authority to ensure that elected councillors play a "key role" in overseeing financial sustainability.

Andrew Burns, deputy chair of the Accounts Commission, said: "There is no doubt about the scale and complexity of the challenges that Glasgow City Council faces, particularly equal pay and homelessness."

He added: "We need to see leadership, responsibility and robust oversight by councillors."

Glasgow City Council depute leader Ricky Bell said the issues raised were "not a surprise".

The SNP councillor said: "The Accounts Commission recognises that many of those challenges are not unique to Glasgow – and that others, such as the pressure on homelessness budgets, are not of the city's making."

He added that the council had made significant progress on a new pay and grading system since the period the Accounts Commission examined.

Scottish Labour local government spokesman Joe Fagan said the report painted a "stark picture about the challenges faced by Glasgow".

He added: "The budget gap will likely require very difficult decisions to be made, which will impact on people living right across the city."

Scottish Conservative local government spokesman Alexander Burnett said Glasgow had been left with a "staggering blackhole" in its finances

He added: "Local people will be left facing swingeing cuts and higher council tax bills because of the SNP's mismanagement."

articles.title: Could Brussels sprouts be off the menu this Christmas?
articles.summary: An Oxfordshire farmer says his Brussels sprouts are under threat from pests after long hot summer.
articles.body:
Love them or hate them you will probably find some sprouts on your plate for Christmas. Whether you choose to eat them however is up to you.

But one organic farmer in Oxfordshire has said the intense heat has created perfect conditions for a 'plague' of flea beetles that, unlike some, love to feast on the brassica.

George Bennet said his sprouts are "touch and go" after a year that has, "really pushed us to the limits". But fear not, there may still be hope for any Brussels buffs out there.

"We will still have Brussels sprouts but they are likely to be quite small, not the big ones that are much easier to peel on your Christmas dinner."

The flea beetle is much smaller than a ladybird - about the size of a pinhead

It attacks leafy plants in the brassica family including cabbage, Brussels sprouts and rapeseed

It lays eggs underneath plants in the soil, not on the leaves

Affected plants are peppered with holes and look like they have been "hit by a shotgun"

Bennet worked in IT before he decided to take over from his dad at Sandy Lane Farm in Tiddington, near Thame.

He grows a diverse range of vegetables using an organic system which he said provides better resilience to extreme weather conditions and chooses to sell his produce direct to avoid market pressure.

But, he said the pressure this year has been from flea beetles which have been "really pervasive".

"Typically they are with us after spring and when it just gets into summer. So we have about three or four weeks.

"The flea beetle now has been with us for about 12 weeks."

Flea beetles will eat away at the leaves of brassicas like sprouts.

The extent of their munching on Bennet's crop has seen some of the leaves eaten by as much as 70 percent, which reduces their ability to photosynthesise and give the plant energy it needs to grow.

He said that a lack of water is one of the reasons the beetle likes to eat away at his crops in search of food and moisture.

But other crops like potatoes and squash have done really well, which is why he advocates for a mixed system.

"We farm for all weathers and whatever is thrown at us we can capitalise on it."

"Having eggs not in one basket is definitely the way forward."

Mike Hirons, CEO of Oxfordshire wholesaler, Produce Warriors, said it is too early to say whether we're likely to see an impact on sprout supply.

But he said poor yields had caused prices of other Christmas vegetables like potatoes and broccoli to increase already.

"What we can know is that if our prices have been high through the summer then it would not surprise me if they continue through the winter."

Despite feeling positive about the future in the system he manages, Bennet said support is "absolutely necessary" to help farmers cope with change.

"Our general climate is moving from very variable weather where we didn't need irrigation... to now we actually need irrigation. And that's expensive.

"That's where government support and funding can really help farmers to start putting into place infrastructure so that we can store over-winter rains and use it in the summer."

Last month the government announced funding of up to £15m to build on-farm reservoirs which it said would help farmers become more resilient to future droughts.

It comes after a spring and summer of persistent heat with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C.

The Met Office said on Tuesday that summer 2026 was the hottest on record where drought was declared in all of Wales and more than two-thirds

As for the sprouts, there are no warnings yet to suggest we're likely to see a shortage but according to Bennet they could be smaller - which may not be a bad thing for some this Christmas.

articles.title: Artist 'shocked' by online response to portrait of dying father
articles.summary: Vincent Michael Brown says painting his father dying was "about as emotional as it gets".
articles.body:
An artist who began painting a portrait of his father just before his death said finishing it had been "part of the grieving process".

Vincent Michael Brown, from Warmley, near Bristol, painted his dad "all through" his life and even had one of his portraits shortlisted for the BP Portrait Award.

But when he shared Father Holding On, his final painting of his dad, online, he was "completely shocked by the response".

"Painting my father dying is about as emotional as it gets. I did most of it in tears, but it helped me. So many people wrote to me saying they saw their experience in my painting," he said.

The image attracted hundreds of comments and thousands of likes from people going through a similar experience, as well as care workers and nurses "who recognised that image".

Responding to the Facebook post, Georgina Millington wrote the image had stopped her in her tracks.

"Reminded me so much of my Dad's final days. Beautiful heart-wrenching tribute."

Girls 'ill' after training for Bristol Channel swim

Scientists may have found first hint of dark matter

While Wayne England posted it was "almost too personal and painful to you, for me to view it., many thanked Brown for sharing such a "beautiful" and "powerful" image that "we can all be familiar with".

Karen Perkins posted: "It seems to have touched so many of us who have also lost our dear dads in the same circumstances, staying by their side until they sadly slip away."

And Sophie Weller wrote: "As a vicar, I'm often with people towards the end of life. This is a really moving picture and reminds me of many precious souls. I'm very moved by this."

While Ellen O'Neill simply posted: "This is my Dad's reality right now. So heart-breaking to sit and watch."

Born in Fishponds in Bristol in 1944, Brown said his father, Michael Brown, was a "tough" and "very strong man" who "didn't show much in the way of emotion" and had "overcome all sorts" in his life.

Married with four children, he was the captain of the local skittles team and a life-long supporter of Bristol Rovers.

"My father was a carpenter. He worked very hard, often seven days a week, and he would come home and fall asleep in the chair," Brown said.

"And I would quite often whip out a sketch pad and do some drawings of him."

But following a diagnosis of vascular dementia, Brown said his father changed.

"It took a year-and-a-half at the end, in and out of hospital," he said.

"To watch him become vulnerable and see that side of him that I had never seen before.

"It was the first time I'd really seen him, and it was the first time he told me he loved me - near the end."

In 2025, his father contracted pneumonia and passed away just before his 81st birthday.

"I didn't even cry when he died, and my father meant the world to me.

"I'd already started the picture - it was about a week later, and I thought, 'this isn't right not to shed a tear' because I knew what I felt.

"So I started painting - and I've never done a painting where I was crying throughout painting the picture."

Brown added he had wanted it to be a tribute to his father's determination.

"Right up until the end, he was a real fighter, and that's part of what the painting was about," he said.

"Not just the fact that he died, but he didn't go quietly."

articles.title: Horse racing fixtures at risk after one of the driest summers on record
articles.summary: Dry weather threatens race meetings as trainers and tracks across the West wait for rain.
articles.body:
The dry summer risks disrupting the early months of the horse racing season, with racecourses warning fixtures could be cancelled unless significant rain arrives in the coming weeks.

Tom Ryall, clerk of the course at Wincanton Racecourse in Somerset, said "a constant wet period for the next two months" is needed to make the ground soft enough to race on for their first fixture of the season on 25 October.

Trainer Paul Nicholls, who is based in Ditcheat, Shepton Mallet, said: "It's one of the driest summers I've ever known," which is preventing some horses from running.

"We've had to water pretty much every day throughout the summer," said Jeremy Martin from Salisbury Racecourse.

"The summer months are our core period of racing, so with racing every two weeks we had to keep putting water on the racecourse to keep it in a good condition, otherwise it would get too firm," Martin added.

"This is the most watering that we've had to do in my 26 years of being here."

Fear and anxiety amid rise in religious hate crime

Girls 'ill' after training for Bristol Channel swim

Salisbury is fortunate to have a license allowing them to extract water from a 400ft borehole connected to an aquifer, meaning they have been able to continue watering throughout the summer.

Despite this, Martin says there is "nothing better than natural rain" for keeping the course healthy and that not all courses are able to do the same:

"Racecourses up and down the country, however they get their water, have had to do everything they can to keep their ground safe," he said.

Ryall said it had been "one of the most extreme summers in terms of weather", leaving Wincanton's course "pretty hard" and unfit for racing.

"The forecast is changing and rain looks to be on the horizon, finally, so we're just taking every week as it comes and doing our best rain dance, really," he said.

Wincanton Racecourse cancelled its first meet last October as well as two others in March year due to the lack of rain.

Ryall said the track probably needs 200-250mm of steady rain over the next six to eight weeks to avoid cancelling it again.

While that would be higher than average, Ryall said it would not be unheard of, noting that 160mm of rain fell in September 2024.

He said it would be a "massive disappointment" to lose any fixtures, but especially the 25 October fixture, which is the course's charity race day.

The racecourse does have access to a small reservoir, but this only refills when it rains, and it would be very costly to expand it or build a new one, he said.

"If we felt this was going to become a regular occurrence every summer, we have options to start the season later."

Nicholls said: "The ground is completely burnt up, no grass at all about, it's been very dry, it's been a challenge.

"The winter horses aren't going to be ready to run normally until the middle of October," he said.

"The first big jump meet of the season is Chepstow in early October, they'll need some water soon," he said.

But he said there is hope because of the rain forecast for September.

"Once it rains, and the ground is safe, we'll go, but if it's not safe, we won't be running anywhere.

He added that although the horses have adapted to the hot weather "really well" it has been a challenge to feed them due to the lack of grass.

articles.title: Jersey Met says this summer was warmest on record
articles.summary: Jersey Met says temperatures peaked on 25 June when they hit 39.3C (102.7F).
articles.body:
This summer was the warmest since records began in 1894, the Jersey Met Office has confirmed.

It said the average temperature for June, July and August was 20.5C (68.9F), compared to a 30-year average of 17.7C (63.9F) for these months.

The hottest single day was 25 June during which 39.3C (102.7F) was recorded.

Regional meteorologists said the data was in line with evidence that climate change was driving hotter summers and increasing the likelihood of drier conditions.

The meteorologists said there had been three heatwaves and temperatures had breached 30C (86F) on 13 days during the summer months.

The previous warmest summer, according to Jersey Met, was in 2022, when sensors had detected an average of 19.6C (67.3F) in June, July and August.

Jersey Met said this summer had also been the second sunniest summer on record, with 986 hours of sunshine.

It said the sunniest summer to date had been in 1976 when there had been 999 hours of sunshine and the dullest summer had been in 1927 with 578 hours.

The team said although the summer of 2026 had brought below average rainfall at 106.9mm (4.2in), it had not beaten records.

They said just 9.8mm (0.3in) of rain had fallen in 1976.

The 30-year average between 1991 and 2020 was 158mm (6.2in), the meterologists added.

Unlike large parts of the UK, the lack of rain had not led to drought conditions or hosepipe bans across the islands.

Paul Aked, from Jersey Met, said the summer had born similarities to the famous drought of 1976 , although 2026 had been hotter, with more heatwave periods and higher peak temperatures.

articles.title: Shropshire music shop owner gifts guitars to girls in Dolly's memory
articles.summary: Alex Harris says US superstar Dolly Parton's support for young people inspired him to help girls pursue music.
articles.body:
The owner of a music shop has given away three guitars to young women and girls in memory of Dolly Parton.

Alex Harris, from Big Al's Music Emporium in Wem, Shropshire, said the US country superstar was "an icon and legend of music, but also an incredibly kind person". She died on 25 August, aged 80.

Parton's support for young people in Tennessee and around the world inspired him to help girls in Shropshire pursue music.

When he offered to give away a guitar on Facebook, it led to a massive response, which he described as "mental".

"I've got this little 3/4 guitar up on the wall… I thought I'd give that to a young girl who can't afford to buy one," he said.

"I'll clean it up, put some new strings on it, and put a little thing on Facebook.

"[It had] thousands and thousands of likes, and it got shared everywhere, and people were saying, 'What a wonderful thing to do.'"

"I've ended up giving away three guitars."

Harris said people on social media had also asked how they could get involved.

People have bought items to donate to the girls, as well as guitars, from his website, he added.

"There was a gig bag, there was a tuner, there was a spare set of strings, there was a learn-to-play book," he said.

The music shop owner said one guitar went to an 18-year-old girl who had dwarfism and needed a smaller instrument.

Thanks to donations from customers, she also got a guitar strap, a learn-to-play book, and an electric clip-on tuner.

One of the other girls was in primary school, Harris confirmed.

"She had the little three-quarter that I originally intended to give away, and somebody paid for a nice padded gig bag to go with that, and a learn-to-play book and a capo."

The third girl to receive a guitar was 17-year-old Amelia, who said Parton was a big influence for her.

"I always looked up to her and how she was so confident in herself and how she just always believed in herself," she said.

"I wondered what that would feel like for me in the future - to be that confident in my abilities."

She added that her grandmother had also been a fan of the singing star and would listen to her music.

It was her mother, though, that spotted the Facebook post and put Amelia forward to receive the guitar.

"It didn't feel real, to be honest; it was really exciting... it was just so cool and just so nice of him," she said of receiving the guitar from Harris.

"I really just want to learn how to play the guitar and one day confidently be able to play songs to my friends and family.

"It's more of a hobby at the moment, but I do really look up to artists, so I'm not sure if that's something I would look at in the future."

articles.title: After his wife of 43 years died, a New York widower looked for companionship online; the woman he met was fake and took $800,000 from his retirement savings
articles.summary: US News: When Simon’s wife of 43 years died, the loss left him struggling with a loneliness he had never known. Like many widows and widowers, he eventually tu.
articles.body: When Simon’s wife of 43 years died, the loss left him struggling with a loneliness he had never known. Like many widows and widowers, he eventually turned online, hoping to find some companionship. Instead, he found Emily. The woman seemed real. The conversations continued and a relationship began to take shape. But Emily did not exist as Simon believed she did. She was part of an online scam, and over the next few months, Simon lost $800,000 from his retirement savings. The money was devastating enough. What followed made matters worse. According to an investigation by The Associated Press and FRONTLINE, Simon was left with $185,000 in borrowed money to repay and tens of thousands of dollars in additional taxes on funds he had withdrawn and subsequently lost. He reported the crime to local police and the FBI, but said he received little meaningful help. Then came another scammer. This time, someone contacted Simon claiming they could connect him with the Secret Service and help recover his stolen money, for an additional fee.His online love was traced to a scam compoundSimon had used the internet looking for something deeply human: connection after bereavement. Instead, he became one of thousands of people caught in increasingly sophisticated online fraud networks.AP and FRONTLINE were able to trace the money stolen from Simon through cryptocurrency wallet addresses and leaked documents to a notorious scam compound in Myanmar. The operation was part of a wider criminal network that targeted victims through different types of online scams. Even after authorities destroyed much of the compound, the scam operations did not disappear. Other sites emerged, leaving Simon no closer to recovering his savings.He has asked that his full name not be published because he remains too ashamed to tell most of his family what happened. That sense of shame is common among victims and it can make an already devastating experience even harder to escape.Americans lost billions to scams in 2025Simon’s experience comes as scams in the United States reach unprecedented levels. Americans reported losing $15.9 billion to fraud in 2025, a 25% increase from the previous year, according to Federal Trade Commission data cited by AP. The agency has also warned that reported figures represent only part of the problem because many victims never report their losses.The FTC separately found that people reported losing $2.1 billion to scams that began on social media in 2025, roughly eight times the amount reported in 2020. Romance scams remain a particularly damaging category, with nearly 60% of people who reported losing money to a romance scam saying it began on a social media platform.The loss doesn’t always end with the moneyFor many victims, recovering stolen funds can be nearly as difficult as the scam itself. In the US, banks generally aren’t required to reimburse customers when they themselves authorised a transaction after being deceived. That leaves victims in a difficult position, particularly when money has been transferred through cryptocurrency or across international borders.Simon’s case illustrates another painful consequence: the financial loss can continue long after the scammer disappears. His retirement savings were gone. He was left with debt and tax liabilities. And when he sought help, another fraudster saw an opportunity to exploit his desperation.The investigation found that this pattern, victims being targeted again by people promising to recover their money, is not unusual. For Simon, the search for companionship began with grief and ended with the loss of a lifetime of savings. What makes his story especially troubling is that the person who deceived him was thousands of miles away, yet the consequences followed him home. articles.body: CHENNAI: Madras high court on Thursday dismissed as not maintainable a plea by DMK chief M K Stalin seeking to nullify the victory of TVK MLA V S Babu from the Kolathur assembly constituency. The plea was moved on the grounds of malfunctioning, mismatch, and discrepancies in the electronic voting machines (EVMs) during post-counting verification.The first bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G Arul Murugan passed the order on Thursday.Stalin had sought 100% counting of the VVPAT and checking and verification of all the 286 electronic voting machines used in the constituency.According to Stalin, he submitted an application for the post-counting checking and verification of the EVMs on May 7. But ECI conducted the exercise only from July 29 after a 45 days-delay.Supreme Court has mandated the ECI to hold the post-counting checking and verification of 5% of the EVMs used in a constituency. Total 14 machines were to be checked, and three of the four machines in the first batch were not functioning; so, another four were selected, of them one was not functioning, he said.He added that since ECI held the check after 45 days’ delay, he could not file an election petition and so the bar under Article 329 of the Constitution will not apply in this case.ECI submitted that the remedy for the petitioner lies in the election petition under section 80 of the Representation of the People Act and not a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution.They noted that there is a bar on such petitions as per Article 329 (B) of the Constitution and that the petitioner should have approached the ECI before the lapse of the 45 days for holding the post-counting check.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: India's growth defies oil shock but data faces credibility questions
articles.summary: India's 7.8% GDP growth has been met with scepticism over methodology and long-term durability due to a weak monsoon.
articles.body:
"Doomsayers were doomed and India bloomed… Yet again," wrote Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on X , reacting to smart first quarter GDP data that came out earlier this week, widely beating forecasts, but also sparking a major controversy over its credibility.

On the face of it, the 7.8% number was a shot in the arm for the prime minister who's recently faced scathing student anger over his government's handling of exam paper leaks and rising youth unemployment.

While those longstanding concerns have not gone anywhere, the better-than-expected growth print suggests that his government may have deftly weathered the Middle East oil shock despite heavy dependencies on imported crude.

According to Sajjid Chinoy, chief India economist at JP Morgan, India's "cyclical growth recovery" had been visible for the past six months, driven by a huge fiscal stimulus, including direct tax cuts in February last year, a reduction of consumption taxes in September and interest rates which have come off by about 1.5% since early 2025.

"But the question was, could India insulate that recovery from events in the Middle East, and this is where the government deserves enormous credit," Mr Chinoy told India Today news channel, adding that the urgency with which Delhi diversified its energy imports in the face of the Hormuz blockade helped the country protect its growth.

What also helped Asia's third largest economy power ahead amid the disruption in global energy markets was a strong acceleration in exports and a surge in private corporate investments, which has long been a point of great concern for economists.

Exports grew by a sharp 12% despite tariff uncertainties on the back of strong global demand and a weak exchange rate. Economists reckon a 15% slump in the Indian rupee against the US dollar may have helped companies improve their competitiveness, driving up demand for Indian goods.

Corporate India, meanwhile, seems to be finally putting money into new buildings and factories. India's gross fixed capital formation, which serves as a core indicator of total domestic public and private investment rose, nearly 12% in the first three months of this year.

"Non-government data also points to the fact that investment intentions of companies have gone up in recent months, with announcements especially concentrated in industries like data centres, renewable energy and metals," Madan Sabnavis, chief economist with the state-run Bank of Baroda, told the BBC.

"Of course, private investment is not broad-based yet, but these are definitely signs of a pick up."

While the robust numbers pushed several private brokerages to revise their full year growth forecasts upwards, they also stirred up a roaring debate online and a war of words between politicians.

Opposition leaders like Jairam Ramesh called the numbers "statistical gymnastics", accusing the government of repeatedly tweaking methodology to conceal what he said was "India's dire economic reality".

A former finance secretary also raised serious doubts, saying the GDP got a pop because it was calculated on the basis of newly revised numbers and a lower base for the same period last year - a view the government strongly rebuffed , saying revisions are a part and parcel of GDP calculations.

The government's view was supported by the World Bank's executive director for the country, Neelkanth Mishra, who said the new GDP series "cleaned up the data and also significantly improved the methodology", enhancing the credibility of the estimates.

But India's new GDP series - a reworked way of measuring the size of the economy - has substantially revised down the estimated level of India's GDP in previous years, automatically making current growth look much higher than it would have been without the revisions.

Beyond the statistical minutiae, others like the former central bank governor Raghuram Rajan have also questioned why if the growth indeed was so rapid was India not creating more jobs or attracting more foreign direct investment.

To make matters worse, the stock markets also largely shrugged off the positive news.

The debate has muddied the picture for authorities who will have hoped the numbers would help them counter growing criticism about the uneven nature of India's growth trajectory.

There are also other more mundane reasons why it might be too early to celebrate a growth bump.

For starters, government spending is expected to ease off in the coming months as the compulsions to meet deficit targets get stronger. The impact of the goods and services tax cuts on spurring consumption is also soon likely to peter out, according to HSBC.

Moreover a sub-par monsoon and El Niño-like weather conditions have taken a toll on India's agrarian rural economy, which supports livelihoods for half of the country. As of 27 August, cumulative rainfall stood at 13% below the long-period average.

This will pose "clear risks to agriculture, rural demand and food inflation [even though] India appears better prepared than in past episodes", CareEdge, a rating agency, said in a note.

Sugar and onion prices have already spiked across the country, forcing the government to run special trains to cities to meet demand. India's retail inflation, meanwhile, hit a 15-month high of 3.9% in May and further rises are expected, with some economists predicting the rate will hit the upper band of the central bank's comfort level amid a weak monsoon.

Given the high-growth and high-inflation scenario, most brokerages are pencilling in a hike in borrowing costs. This, coupled with expectations of lower global growth (and hence lower demand for Indian exports), higher costs of inputs and energy because of volatile geopolitics could all mean this growth bonanza - credible or not - may well be nearing its peak.

articles.summary: KOLKATA: A special team of Bengal Police arrested former Panihati Municipality chairman Somnath Dey in Bengaluru in the early hours of Thursday for hi.
articles.body: KOLKATA: A special team of Bengal Police arrested former Panihati Municipality chairman Somnath Dey in Bengaluru in the early hours of Thursday for his alleged role in the hurried cremation of the RG Kar rape and murder victim and the alleged destruction of evidence.Dey had been absconding, repeatedly changing locations and using multiple phone numbers after Khardah police station registered an FIR based on a complaint filed by the victim’s family on Aug 10.Dey’s name was found on the cremation ground requisition documents. Police will bring him to Bengal on transit remand, produce him before the Barrackpore court and then take him to Khardah police station for questioning to probe the alleged conspiracy and the instructions under which he acted.The victim’s family alleged that Dey misused his administrative power and influence to bypass legal and social procedures and arrange a hurried cremation, with the aim of destroying crucial evidence and disrupting the murder investigation.The Aug 10 FIR followed a directive from Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari to the Barrackpore Police Commissionerate during an Aug 9 memorial meeting at Panihati to examine the events at the cremation ground.Dey is the third person arrested in connection with the FIR. Former Panihati MLA Nirmal Ghosh was arrested at a hotel near Puri in Odisha, while former councillor and neighbour Sanjib Mukhopadhyay was arrested at a house in Chinar Park, Kolkata.Both were granted bail in this case, although Ghosh remains in jail in connection with a separate case.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.title: Ossett boutique owners photos stolen to sell weight loss drugs
articles.summary: Images from Ossett clothing boutique's account were doctored and overlaid with fake captions.
articles.body:
A mother and daughter who run a clothing shop said they felt “helpless” when their promotional photos were stolen and manipulated to sell weight loss drugs on social media.

The images of Nicola Dexter modelling outfits were lifted without consent and altered to make her appear overweight.

They were then posted on a TikTok account as “before” and “after” photos alongside false claims that Nicola had taken a weight loss treatment called Pinkies.

TikTok removed the account when contacted by the BBC and said: "We have banned this account for breaching our community guidelines."

Nicola and her daughter Antonia set up Style by Eleven during the Covid pandemic.

They have built a loyal customer base, both at their shop in Ossett, Wakefield, and online.

Nicola models for their website and social media pages, while Antonia takes the pictures and manages their online presence.

Antonia said: “About a month ago a customer messaged us to say, ‘Have you seen this on TikTok?’

“We hadn’t, but there were loads of videos of my mum promoting this drug.

“They were her but they had been manipulated, possibly by AI, and then they’d used her actual pictures to say ‘this is what I look like now’. ”

The account included a link to an external website where capsules and "food noise patches" could be purchased.

Antonia started by reporting each post to TikTok, but each time she was told that it hadn’t violated community guidelines.

She filled out a full report on the website and had an online chat, but was told again that the account and the posts didn’t violate guidelines.

Antonia also wrote to TikTok's legal team.

The pair had been fighting to get the account removed for about a month before the BBC got involved.

Nicola said: “It wasn’t what they had done to me, I am quite thick-skinned, I was more worried about the people buying them.

“What were they buying? Had they taken money out of people‘s bank accounts?

“What were they getting? They were using us to promote something we knew nothing about.”

Liz Ward, an intellectual property specialist at Virtuoso Legal in Leeds, said there was very little Antonia and Nicola could do from a legal perspective.

“The problem is that there are no image rights in the UK, so enforcing your rights as an entity is quite difficult.

“There are civil remedies, they can go to the court and ask for a remedy for "passing off" and copyright infringement too.

“But, of course, it all takes a lot of money and that’s the difficulty.

“I think the other difficulty is they don’t know who the potential defendant would be.”

Ward was referring to potential issues in tracing the people running the account selling the Pinkies products.

She said she thinks the law should be changed to allow criminal proceedings for this kind of illicit use of someone’s image.

She also thinks the social media platforms should be held more accountable.

“The platforms use a lot of automated responses, this is a problem we have, although we manage to overcome it in most cases by writing as a lawyer.

“But for a lot of people who want take down notices, it should be quick, it should be easy, but they’re never reviewed by a human being, so a lot of criminal activity is really going unchecked.

“So, arguably, the platforms are aiding and abetting that criminal activity.”

When the BBC contacted TikTok to highlight the problem the social media platform responded almost immediately and within a few hours the account had been removed.

TikTok added in a statement: "Our terms of service and community guidelines clearly state that users are prohibited from posting, sharing, or sending any content that violates or infringes on another user's copyrights, trademarks, or other intellectual property rights.

"We also do not allow content that promotes disordered eating, risky weight loss or muscle gain methods, or harmful body comparisons. We also have strict rules against trading, marketing, or providing access to regulated, prohibited, or high-risk goods and services."

Nicola said their customers were supportive and tried to help get the posts removed.

She said: “It is just humiliating to us. We felt helpless and it has taken something away from us. They have stolen my picture and my identity.

The mother and daughter duo said the ordeal has not put them off posting photos, because they need an online presence for their business.

But Antonia said it would stop her buying products she saw promoted on TikTok.

“There are all these innocent people commenting asking where they can buy the products because they are believing what they are seeing.

“It’s just really worrying that TikTok are allowing their users to be scammed, really.”

articles.title: ‘Mayday emergency’: IndiGo Doha-Bengaluru flight diverts to Muscat after pilot falls ill mid-air
articles.summary: MUMBAI: An IndiGo flight from Doha to Bengaluru was diverted to Muscat on Thursday after one of its pilots was reportedly incapacitated mid-flight, pr.
articles.body: MUMBAI: An IndiGo flight from Doha to Bengaluru was diverted to Muscat on Thursday after one of its pilots was reportedly incapacitated mid-flight, prompting the aircraft to declare a Mayday emergency, said sources.The A320neo aircraft operating flight 6E 1302 took off from Doha at 3am, about an hour behind schedule, according to data from a flight-tracking website. Less than two hours later, the aircraft turned towards Muscat to carry out an approach and landing.Pilot incapacitation is treated as a serious in-flight emergency, as it means one of the pilots becomes unable to continue performing their duties. Aircraft such as those in the Airbus A320 family are operated by two pilots on the flight deck. If one becomes incapacitated, the other pilot can continue flying the aircraft.However, this would mean single-handedly managing all the duties normally shared between the two pilots on the flight deck, including flying and monitoring the aircraft, navigating, communicating with air traffic control, managing the aircraft’s systems and responding to abnormal or emergency situations.Since this can significantly increase the workload on the remaining pilot, pilot incapacitation is treated as an emergency. It can prompt the crew to divert to a suitable nearby airport, where the incapacitated pilot can receive medical attention and the flight can continue with a replacement crew.In a statement, IndiGo confirmed that the diversion was necessitated by an urgent requirement for medical attention for one operating crew member. The crew member was attended to by a medical team after landing and was reported to be feeling better, the airline added.The airline said an alternate aircraft and a new set of crew had been arranged to continue the journey to Bengaluru. articles.title: Colorado farmer Marc Arnusch turned down solar leases on 2,700 acres; instead he chose a conservation easement to protect the family farm, then faced an IRS audit
articles.summary: US News: Colorado farmer Marc Arnusch had a straightforward choice: accept millions of dollars from solar companies seeking to lease 2,700 acres of his family’.
articles.body: Colorado farmer Marc Arnusch had a straightforward choice: accept millions of dollars from solar companies seeking to lease 2,700 acres of his family’s farmland, or keep the property in agriculture for the next generation. He chose the farm. Now, after spending nearly $1 million documenting a conservation easement, he is facing an IRS audit over the tax deduction associated with it. Reporting by Just the News, recent statements from the Internal Revenue Service and reporting by Colorado Public Radio help illuminate the dispute and the broader debate over conservation easements. Arnusch, a third-generation farmer in Weld County, said the solar offers were tempting but ultimately incompatible with what he wanted for the land.Instead, his family pursued a conservation easement, a legal agreement that permanently limits certain uses of privately owned land in order to protect its conservation values. Federal law allows qualifying conservation easements to generate charitable tax deductions, provided the statutory requirements are met.The decision required extensive documentation. Arnusch’s family hired roughly a dozen specialists, including tax attorneys, engineers, solar experts, mineral geologists and land-use professionals. Soil testing, core samples, zoning and boundary surveys and other studies were used to establish what is known as the property’s “highest and best use”, an appraisal concept that considers the most valuable use that is legally permissible, physically possible and financially feasible.The solar companies’ interest in the property was part of that equation. Their offers provided evidence that solar development could represent a significant economic use of the land. An independent appraisal was then prepared using the information gathered by the family’s experts. Arnusch claimed a tax deduction based on the resulting valuation, although he says he has not yet been able to use the full deduction because he did not have sufficient income.Then, roughly three years after the deduction was claimed, the IRS opened an audit. According to Arnusch, an IRS employee visited the farm, and he questioned whether the person conducting the review had the expertise necessary to evaluate such a complicated property.Arnusch said the family had relied on numerous experts throughout the process, but the IRS later sent an auditor who, according to Arnusch, was conducting their first audit of a farm. The IRS did not respond to requests for comment.Arnusch’s experience is part of a much larger fight over conservation-easement valuations. Critics of the IRS’s approach argue that government reviews can reach dramatically lower valuations than those produced by taxpayers who commission extensive expert studies.Bernie Donachie, a value-analytics specialist with interests in conservation-easement properties, examined 10 publicly available cases. He found that taxpayers’ experts had collectively valued the properties at $358.2 million, while IRS valuations totaled about $1.57 million, a reduction of roughly 99 percent, according to his analysis reported by Just the News. Those figures represent Donachie’s sample, not an official governmentwide assessment.The controversy comes against the backdrop of years of IRS enforcement involving conservation easements. The agency has argued that legitimate conservation deductions should be protected while abusive transactions and inflated valuations should not receive tax benefits. Now, the IRS is changing how it handles the issue.On Aug. 19, the agency announced the creation of an Office of Conservation Easements, saying the new office will centralize technical expertise and coordinate policy, enforcement and case-resolution strategies involving conservation and historic-preservation easements. The IRS simultaneously ended its current uniform settlement initiative, saying standardized settlement letters were not suited to the variety of cases it was handling.For taxpayers with pending cases, the change does not automatically mean their disputes will disappear. The IRS says they can continue seeking settlements through their assigned examination or Chief Counsel representatives, with individual cases potentially resolved on different terms depending on the circumstances and litigation risks.For Arnusch, however, the issue is more personal than a dispute over a tax bill. He chose conservation because he wanted his family’s land to remain a farm rather than become a solar development. Now he is waiting to see whether the government will accept the valuation that helped him make that choice.He does not want to keep fighting the government; he simply wants to protect the farm. For a family that has spent generations working the same ground, the question is whether preserving that future will ultimately come with a tax price they cannot afford.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: EU remains divided over trade sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements
articles.summary: Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee says the bloc ‘should be moving collectively’ in upholding international law.
articles.body:
European Union foreign ministers remain divided after talks on imposing trade sanctions against Israel amid increasing settler violence in the occupied West Bank.

Ireland, the current holder of the EU council presidency, hosted an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in Wicklow on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Reporting from Wicklow, Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith said Ireland and Spain, with the support of Belgium and the Netherlands, led the call for EU-wide restrictions against goods imported from illegal Israeli settlements at the meeting.

He said that Germany, Austria, Czechia and Hungary are clear that they would oppose any attempts to sanction illegal settlements, saying such a move would upset diplomatic channels with Israel.

Ireland was the first EU country to ban imported Israeli settlement goods. The country recognised a Palestinian state in 2024 amid Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza and continues to criticise Israel’s expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Ireland has also pushed for a review of the EU-Israel Association Agreement, a cooperation deal signed in 2000 that forms the basis for trade ties with Israel.

The EU bloc is Israel’s largest trading partner as bilateral trade of goods reached nearly $50bn last year. The volume of trade has increased since 2023. EU exports to Israel increased from nearly $30bn to about $32bn in 2025.

“We should be moving collectively … It is not credible for us to say we should uphold international law in one form and not do it in the other,” Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee told reporters after the meeting.

“We’re hearing that at the meetings of the foreign ministers in Wicklow this week, only Ireland raised the issue of the illegal settlements,” Irish Member of the European Parliament Lynn Boylan told Al Jazeera.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas did not address the prospect of trading sanctions in a news conference after the informal meeting.

She previously commented on proposals to curb trade with illegal Israeli settlements at a previous Gymnich meeting in July and said at the time that the ministers debated three options, which included an import licensing system, prohibitive tariffs or a ban, Reuters reported.

Kallas said at the time that a plan for a ban received the strongest backing at the gathering that took place in Brussels, but there was no clear majority for any single option.

There is also debate on whether the imposition of trade restrictions requires unanimity from the ministers. EU trade decisions can be passed by a simple majority vote, but major political or policy decisions require a unanimous vote.

Several protesters demonstrated near the golf resort where the meeting was held and were seen holding signs that read “You need to boycott Israel now” and “Sanction Israel”.
